sections.overview: Idaea flaveolaria is a small geometrid moth associated in Europe with alpine habitats. French naturalist records place it in the Alpine massif, where its bright coloration makes it noticeable in sunny mountain meadows. Its caterpillar and feeding ecology are much less well known than its adult appearance and distribution.
sections.identification: Adult wingspan is about 12–16 mm. No dependable body mass or measured body-width data were found in the specialist references consulted; male and female wingspans are not separated there. The adult is a small moth with vivid yellow-orange to warm-brown wings and fine transverse lines that may be clearer underneath; a dark discal spot can also show below. The combination of color and markings helps separate it from similar Idaea, but worn specimens and locality still matter.
sections.habitat: In France, the species is recorded from the Alpine massif; European records are likewise associated with mountain regions. French observations describe sunny, flower-rich high-altitude meadows. This is a localized alpine distribution, not a general species of lowland gardens or farmland.
sections.diet: The larva is thought to be polyphagous, but its food plants and feeding behavior have not been observed adequately in the field according to the French species account. Adult feeding details are not established in the sources reviewed. The food-plant gap is therefore part of the species’ known natural-history uncertainty.
sections.behavior: Adults may be seen flying in sunshine over alpine meadows. The French observatory describes this as a sun-loving, conspicuous small moth. Detailed observations of daily activity, courtship and overwintering stages were not available in the sources used for this profile.
sections.reproduction: The sources reviewed do not document the egg, larval and pupal schedule of I. flaveolaria in enough detail to describe it confidently. The caterpillar’s natural food plants and habits are explicitly noted as unobserved, so a fuller breeding account would be speculative.
sections.ecology: The species is part of the alpine moth community and is linked to sunny meadow habitat. The French observatory considers it rare at the scale of its recording grid and notes that larval ecology remains unresolved. No specific pollination, prey or population effect is quantified by the reviewed sources.
sections.conservation: A French moth observatory describes the species as rare on its survey grid and its French distribution as limited to the Alps. That local observation is not a global conservation assessment. No verified global IUCN category or population trend was found for this profile.
